name: Beth Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We keep this confidential. What fills an ordinary shift for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a power line crew for an electricity company, checking isolation plans, repairing faults and making sure the younger workers know why we stop a job. My technical diploma helps with the plans, but a line in the rain teaches its own lessons. The work is good; the pay is low for a crew lead, and my partner and I count every mortgage payment around our two children’s school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a modest AI tool might tidy the depot paperwork. I use one now and then to check wording, but the pole, the tester and our own eyes decide the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not have the money to be easy about anything. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few nearby lineworker jobs even for someone who can lead a crew. A tidy AI job note cannot clear my mortgage debit or test a power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the lead shifts and available callouts. Starting this month, I would put forty from each callout payment into a new emergency account, and in the first year I would keep checking any AI wording against the job sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, as usual. The mild AI picture does not threaten the line, but it does not raise my low pay either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first bill you check after a callout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check whether the mortgage debit has cleared, then the children’s school meal balance. If the callout pays, I move forty to emergency savings before the rest gets spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error do you look for in an AI drafted job note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tool can make a repair sound finished when a second inspection is still due. I compare the draft with the signed job sheet before I send anything.

say: A **little** AI can tidy notes while field workers still decide if a line is safe.
I would **keep** crew checks and work from the signed job sheet.
think: Our **thin** savings and lower crew lead pay keep the mortgage stressful even without major AI change.
**Few** nearby lineworker vacancies make a pay gap hard to solve quickly.
do: **Keep** lead shifts and verify any AI wording against signed job sheets.
**Move** forty from each actual callout payment into emergency savings.
feel: **Anxious** over existing bills, with little added fear from modest AI.
S0.quote: A tidy AI job note cannot clear my mortgage debit or test a power line.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI only occasionally and checks it against signed field records.
**New** saving comes from actual callout pay; her existing cushion remains under a month.

steps.text: Keep crew lead shifts and check drafted notes against signed job sheets
Save forty from each paid callout into emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster dispatch is worth a look if the company lets a crew correct a bad order. I would not buy a system that counts travel time but forgets a damaged pole needs a second person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose routine scheduling work while field repair continues, but fewer planners could mean fewer callouts for us too. I need those paid hours to keep the mortgage current; I cannot live on the little we have saved. A faster dispatch board is no bargain if a power line crew arrives without the right parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for a one-month side-by-side trial of the new dispatch schedule and the old board. In the first year I would log any lost callout hours, then put the evidence to management with a request for a fair lead rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can judge a trial on its results. I learned to change a method when it proves safer, not because a sales pitch sounded clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof the schedule helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare actual arrival times and whether each repair had the right crew and parts. A few faster routes would not offset repeated missing equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you do if the lead rate stays low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep this job while I ask the few nearby electricity companies about real vacancies and pay. I would not resign before a written offer because our savings are too thin.

say: I would **trial** dispatch software against real arrival times, parts and crew needs.
I would **request** a fair lead rate if callout hours shrink.
think: **Office** automation could reduce planners and paid field callouts before robots touch the lines.
A **thin** cushion makes even a modest hours cut serious for our mortgage.
do: **Compare** new dispatch schedule with old board for one month.
**Log** lost callout hours and request a fair lead rate from management.
**Ask** nearby electricity companies about actual paid lead vacancies if the rate stays low.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours, though willing to judge a proven tool.
S1.quote: A faster dispatch board is no bargain if a power line crew arrives without the right parts.
fieldNote: Her **acceptance** of change depends on measured arrival times and complete crews.
She would **search** locally only if low lead pay persists, and would wait for a written offer before leaving.

steps.text: Trial dispatch schedule against old board for one month
Ask nearby companies about lead vacancies if current rate stays low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our team that thinking AI by 2028 may take scheduling first, and capable robots around 2031 may reach the pole. I want a proven field test and a paid worker beside every robot until it earns trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot taking our callout hours would leave a hole in the mortgage money almost at once. I am good at leading repairs, but less than a month’s savings and few local openings mean I cannot simply walk away. A line robot can wait for its next software fix; my mortgage cannot wait for its next pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would gather our household bills with my partner this week and stop the paid sports subscription. Before 2028 I would request paid robot observation shifts from the company, and in the first year after thinking AI arrives I would take any funded practical course tied to an actual line safety post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, although I can still list what needs doing. I am not afraid of a useful machine; I am afraid of a gap between wages ending and new wages starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask before taking that practical course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the company to pay my time and show me the posted safety job and its wage. If it pays less than our mortgage and school costs require, I stay on line shifts and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner say about cutting sports?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would rather keep the children’s school activities and lose the channel. We would make the decision together after looking at the actual bills.

say: I would **demand** proven field tests and paid workers beside early line robots.
**Thinking** AI may change dispatch by 2028 before robots reach power lines around 2031.
think: **Callout** loss could threaten our mortgage quickly because savings cover less than a month.
My **lead** skill cannot create nearby vacancies or bridge an unpaid course.
do: **Review** household bills and cancel the sports subscription with my partner.
**Take** funded safety course after 2028 only if a posted job pays enough.
feel: **Alarmed** about an immediate wage gap despite a practical response.
S2.quote: A line robot can wait for its next software fix; my mortgage cannot wait for its next pay packet.
fieldNote: She is **willing** to learn from a field trial, but refuses an unpaid leap.
The **course** depends on company funding and an actual job with pay sufficient for household costs.

steps.text: Cancel sports subscription after reviewing family bills
Request paid robot observation shifts before 2028
Take funded line safety course after 2028 if posted job covers costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the years to 2031 for thinking AI and 2034 for robots should be spent proving field safety, not buying promises. A crew lead with a diploma should be able to inspect the repair a machine leaves behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn inspection if someone shows it working on real faults first. The children will still need school money, and our savings are thin, so I cannot trade a regular low wage for no wage during training. A robot inspection certificate is useful only if the power line company pays me while I earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for the company’s inspection course dates, paid hours and posted job rate. If training is paid and an inspection opening meets our mortgage and school costs, I would enroll before 2031 and apply for the opening when posted; otherwise I would keep leading the line crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less cornered than in the two-year picture. More time matters only if the training has a wage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What real fault would you want in the inspection course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a damaged crossarm and a missing isolation marker, not a clean training yard. An inspector should be able to stop a machine when its plan misses either one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move home for the inspection role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a speculative vacancy. My partner’s work and the children’s school are here, so I would need a firm local offer before considering any change.

say: I would **support** inspection training based on actual faults before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would **ask** for paid hours and a posted job rate.
think: A **diploma** helps me learn inspection, but unpaid training would worsen the family’s cash gap.
A **local** opening needs to cover mortgage and school costs before I change roles.
do: **Ask** company for inspection course dates, paid hours and job rate.
**Enroll** before 2031 if course is paid and suitable local inspection post is posted.
**Apply** when posted inspection opening covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** but less trapped when there is time for a paid path.
S3.quote: A robot inspection certificate is useful only if the power line company pays me while I earn it.
fieldNote: Her **openness** to training is conditional on field proof, paid hours and a real local post.
She does **not** propose moving her partner and children for an uncertain vacancy.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if inspection course is paid and suitable local post exists
Apply for local inspection opening if pay covers mortgage and school costs
Keep leading power line crew if paid path does not materialise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and roughly three more years before capable robots gives apprentices time to learn with the machines. I would like a paid master trainer role that keeps practical line repair in the lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three, I might welcome fewer storm callouts, but there is no promised retirement cheque in my plan. We need to build savings from current pay first, and a trainer wage would still have to cover the mortgage if we have one. An apprentice should meet the damaged power line before meeting the robot’s answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the apprenticeship office this year about the assessor qualification and actual trainer vacancies. If a paid assessor course and a local trainer opening at a suitable wage appear, I would take the course within five years and apply for the opening; I would also set aside twenty from each normal weekly wage starting now. I would apply for the local trainer opening if its pay covers our family costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy because our finances are still tight, though the long timetable gives us a workable sequence. I would rather teach a proper isolation check than watch a machine make the same hidden mistake twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprentices do with a robot in your lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would inspect the pole and name the hazard before looking at the robot plan. A screen answer should be the second opinion, not the first thing a new worker believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why twenty a week instead of more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty is what our current lower pay can spare after mortgage and school costs. If a week is short, I would skip the transfer rather than borrow to make it.

say: I would **seek** paid practical teaching that keeps isolation checks in apprenticeships.
The **decade** permits steady preparation before capable robots reach lines around 2039.
think: A **trainer** role may reduce storm nights but still must pay the household bills.
**Current** low pay and thin savings need attention long before any robot arrives.
do: **Ask** apprenticeship office about assessor qualification and real local trainer posts.
**Take** paid assessor course within five years if suitable local trainer opening appears.
**Save** twenty from each normal weekly wage when household bills allow.
feel: **Uneasy** about present finances, with more room to plan than under fast AGI.
S4.quote: An apprentice should meet the damaged power line before meeting the robot’s answer.
fieldNote: Her **long** view favours paid apprenticeships and household saving from current wages.
**Despite** more preparation time, thin savings and low pay keep her anxious about the near term.

steps.text: Take paid assessor course within five years if suitable local trainer opening appears
Apply for local trainer opening if pay covers family costs
Save twenty from weekly wages when bills allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could cut the paid callouts by around 2031, and our savings would not cover a lost month. Paid field observation and training linked to a real local job would help. A power line worker cannot train through an unpaid month when the mortgage is already due.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the young workers get a proper apprenticeship if the easiest repairs go to a robot. I learned from someone who let me check a line and then explained my mistake. That teaching needs paid time, not a spare minute at the end of a callout.

headlineQuote: A power line worker cannot train through an unpaid month when the mortgage is already due.
portrait: **Beth** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and strong field judgement on damaged lines.
Her **partner**, two school-age children and mortgage depend on lower-than-usual lineworker pay, with less than one month saved.
She **uses** AI occasionally, tests new methods when proven, and prefers paid apprenticeships and family budgeting over promises.
**Few** nearby jobs make her require funded courses and real local offers before leaving line repair for inspection or teaching.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots around 2031 and cut callouts before her thin cushion can absorb lost pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field observation and training tied to a real local job with enough pay would give her a viable route.
